newsitem.title: USA: Sony hires adviser for studio - report.
newsitem.headline: Sony hires adviser for studio - report.

text.p: Sony Corp. has hired CS First Boston to advise it on options for its troubled Hollywood studio, and wants to take the business public, the Daily Variety said in its Tuesday edition.

The trade paper said Sony Corp. president Nobuyuki Idei addressed senior Sony Pictures Entertainment executives on Monday and ruled out persistent rumors that the Japanese electronics giant wanted to exit Hollywood altogether.

CS First Boston is expected to help Sony focus on long-term strategic issues for the studio, including whether to bring in a minority partner and how to expand the business into areas like cable programming, the paper said. CS First Boston is a unit of CS Holding.

Sony paid $3.4 billion for the Culver City, California, based studio in 1989 in an ill-fated attempt to seek "synergy" between its own electronics hardware and the studio's entertainment software. The plan soon foundered and Sony took an embarrassing $3.2 billion write-off two years ago.
Persistent management problems and weak movies culminated in a disastrous summer at the box office where Sony flopped with such films as "Multiplicity," "The Cable Guy," "The Fan" and "Matilda."
In recent months, Sony cleaned out the executive suites at the studio, installing United Artists president John Calley as president and chief operating officer.

He replaced Alan Levine. Other departures include that of Columbia-TriStar Motion Picture Group chairman Mark Canton, Columbia Pictures president Lisa Henson, TriStar Pictures president Marc Platt and marketing head Sid Ganis.
Daily Variety quoted sources at Idei's meeting as saying he was confident the company would go public, a process that would likely take two years.
One source said Idei likes the movie business and wants advice on how to fix it, preferably in a low-cost way, the paper said.

Mindful of the narrow focus of its entertainment business, Idei wants the studio to use its library to expand in areas like cable programming, by starting new cable networks or buying existing networks.

Idei also wants to focus less on deals and more on movies, listing some of his personal favorites such as "The Godfather," the "Die Hard" franchise, "Always" and "The Remains of the Day," the paper added.
